title: The For Loop
description: Repeat an action many times without writing it out again and again.

content.real: Writing a line 100 times by hand
content.code:
for i in range(100):
    print("I will not throw paper airplanes")
content.text: By hand, writing 'I will not throw paper airplanes' one hundred times takes an afternoon. A **loop** lets you write the action once and tell Python how many times to repeat it.

items.sub: Write it once, run it many times.
The most common loop. It repeats a set number of times.
Tells the `for` loop how many times to go round.

parts.label: counter
parts.note: A variable that holds which turn you are on.

parts.label: colon
parts.note: Ends the loop line. The repeated lines come next, indented.

steps.note: The loop starts. Turn 1: `i` is set to `0`.
Back to the top. Turn 2: `i` becomes `1`.
Back to the top. Turn 3: `i` becomes `2`.
Run the indented line a third time.
`range(3)` has no numbers left, so the loop ends.

content.title: Watch the loop go round
content.outro: One `print` line, three lines of output.

content.question: How many lines does this print?
content.explain: `range(4)` makes the loop go round 4 times, and each turn prints one line.

items: Look at the space in front of `print` inside the loop.
That space is called **indentation**. Press Tab or type four spaces.
The indented lines are the ones that get repeated.
Indentation is how Python knows which lines belong inside the loop.
content.title: Inside or outside?

items.title: Inside the loop
items.text: `Hop` is indented, so it repeats. `Done` is not, so it runs once, after the loop.

items.title: Error
items.text: Nothing is indented, so Python cannot tell what to repeat. It stops with an `IndentationError`.

content.title: Indented vs not indented
content.caption: If you forget to indent the line inside the loop, Python stops with an error, because it cannot tell which lines you meant to repeat.

content.question: What does this print?
options: A, B, A, B, C (each on its own line)
A, B, C, A, B, C
content.explain: `A` and `B` are both indented, so both repeat on each of the 2 turns. `C` is not indented, so it prints once at the end.
content.code:
for i in range(2):
    print("A")
    print("B")
print("C")

items: The `i` in the loop is a variable that holds which turn you are on.
Python fills it in for you on every repeat.
You can print it like any other variable.
content.title: Meet i

content.code:
for i in range(3):
    print("Repeat number:", i)

steps.note: Print the text, then the value inside `i`.
Turn 2. Python changes `i` to `1` for you.
Same line, but `i` holds something new.
No numbers left in `range(3)`. The loop is done.

content.title: Watch i change
content.outro: Three turns, and `i` went 0, 1, 2. It never reached 3.

content.value:
for i in range(5):
    print("Repeat number:", i)
The counter does not have to be called `i`. Any variable name works, and a clear one often reads better: `for floor in range(5):`.

content.question: What is the last number this prints?
content.explain: `range(4)` gives `0, 1, 2, 3`. It starts at 0, so the last number is 3, not 4.

content.value: Choosing Where to Start and Stop

parts.label: stop
parts.note: Counting stops **before** this number. You never get it.

parts.label: step
parts.note: How much to jump each time. A negative step counts backwards.

content.title: Anatomy of range with three numbers
content.caption: `range` always stops **before** the stop number, never on it. That is why `range(5)` gives five numbers but the last one is 4.

content.value: Turn the dials below to see exactly which numbers come out.

content.question: Which numbers does `range(2, 8, 2)` give?
content.explain: Start at 2, jump by 2, and stop before 8. So you get 2, 4 and 6.

editorCode:
for i in range(5):

practice.question: Use a for loop to print your favourite food 4 times. Replace the pass line with your print.
practice.starterCode:
for i in range(4):
    pass    # replace this line with your print

practice.question: Print the numbers 1 to 10 using range with two numbers.
practice.starterCode:
for i in range(1, 11):
    pass    # replace this line with print(i)

quiz.question: What does a loop do?
options: It repeats an action over and over.
It makes the computer shut down.
quiz.explain: A loop repeats the same action again and again, so you do not have to copy and paste the code.

quiz.question: Why do we indent the line inside a loop?
options: To make the code look pretty.
To tell Python which line should be repeated.
quiz.explain: The indentation tells Python exactly which lines belong inside the loop and should be repeated.

quiz.question: Which numbers does range(1, 4) give you?
quiz.explain: With two numbers, range starts at the first and stops before the second. So range(1, 4) gives 1, 2, 3.
